correctness.rationale: The two involute steps are linear and translation-equivariant by the published formulas. Every vector in the closed double-polygon edge space is realized as the central equidistant of a convex constant-width polygon after adding a sufficiently large multiple of U, so the published convergence theorem applies to every vector in that space. Hence the induced shape map A has A^k x -> 0 for all x, which implies spectral radius below 1 and makes I-A invertible. Iterating the affine decomposition then yields the claimed finite translation-cocycle sum. Exact rational replay in verify.py confirms the nontrivial indexing and sign conventions; no finite experiment is used for the general proof.

The 2017 discrete-cycloid paper linearizes shape/radius data only up to translation, so it does not determine this absolute center. The 2015/2017 Arnold et al. work uses different perpendicular- and angular-bisector discretizations. Targeted published-finding corpus and primary-literature searches found no statement implying the translation-cocycle formula.

value.rationale: The foundational paper poses direct recovery of the central point as an explicit open question. The result gives a complete finite procedure for every convex polygon: one constructs a single double-involute operator on an (n-2)-dimensional space and solves one linear system. It also identifies why later curvature-radius operator methods alone do not answer the question: they quotient out the translation that the new cocycle B recovers. This is a natural structural closure of a named gap, not a routine parameter increment or arbitrary special case.
